subject: Architecture
title: Mexico City: A City Sinking Into Its Lake
description: A micro-lesson that makes Mexico City: A City Sinking Into Its Lake usable.

hook.text: Mexico City is sinking up to 20 inches per year — because it was built on a drained lake bed.

buildup.text: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlán sat on Lake Texcoco. Spanish conquerors drained the lake and built on top.

discovery.text: Pumping groundwater for 21 million residents compresses the clay — causing buildings to sink unevenly.

twist.text: The Palace of Fine Arts has sunk over 16 feet since 1934. Stairs had to be added to reach the sinking entrance.

climax.text: The sinking makes the city more vulnerable to earthquakes — soft lake sediment amplifies seismic shaking.

punchline.text: They drained a lake and built a city. Now the city is becoming the lake again.

quiz.question: Why is Mexico City sinking?
options: Tectonic plates are pulling the ground downward
Groundwater pumping compresses the clay lake bed beneath it
Heavy buildings are crushing the rocky foundation

details.summary: Mexico City was built on the drained lakebed of Lake Texcoco, and the soft clay beneath is compressing as groundwater is extracted. The city has sunk over 10 meters in some areas, causing buildings to lean, pipes to crack, and the iconic Palace of Fine Arts to descend into the earth.
details.whyItMatters: Mexico City shows what happens when a civilization builds on geology it doesn't fully understand. Its ongoing subsidence damages infrastructure faster than it can be repaired, creating an escalating cycle of expense and risk.
takeaways: Mexico City is built on a drained lakebed of soft clay
Groundwater extraction has caused over 10 meters of subsidence
Buildings lean and infrastructure cracks from ongoing settling

faq.question: Why was Mexico City built on a lake?
faq.answer: The Aztec capital Tenochtitlán was built on an island in Lake Texcoco. Spanish conquistadors drained the lake and built Mexico City on top. The remaining clay lakebed compresses as groundwater is pumped out, causing the entire city to sink unevenly at rates up to 50 cm per year in some zones.

faq.question: Can Mexico City stop sinking?
faq.answer: Only by eliminating groundwater extraction, which requires massive investment in alternative water supply. The city has made progress but still pumps heavily. Even if extraction stopped today, continued consolidation of the clay would cause sinking for decades, though at reduced rates.
